title: OpenVDDK – Independent Virtual Disk Library
excerpt: An independent, open-source drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, written from scratch. Read-only HotAdd, NBDSSL and NBD on Linux. Apache 2.0; download the user or developer kit on GitHub.
content_html:
Open source · Apache 2.0 · HotAdd, NBDSSL and NBD

Independent Virtual Disk Library
Drop-in. Written from scratch.

OpenVDDK is an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.

Note: the README inside the 0.7.4 download lists vSphere 6.7, 7.0 and 8.0. vSphere 9.1.1 was tested after the release (see "Where it stands"). We don't change released files, so their published SHA-256 checksums, and installers that rely on them, stay valid. The next release carries the updated list.

Your application doesn't have to know

An application that loads libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3 doesn't need to know whether it got VMware's VDDK or OpenVDDK: same file name, same functions, same calls, same data back. No rewrite and no new integration path. In our tests, the difference applications noticed was the timing.

Same file, same interface

The same shared object name and the same exported VixDiskLib functions. Replace the file and restart the service.

HotAdd

Attaches the snapshot disk to your proxy VM, finds and verifies it in the guest, reads it and hands it back. An interrupted run is cleaned up by the next one.

NBDSSL and NBD

Reads the disk directly from the ESXi host over NBDSSL or NBD, without a HotAdd proxy VM. NBDSSL encrypts the connection. Only the transports you request are used: an NBDSSL-only request never falls back to clear-text NBD. A disk can be read over several NFC sessions at once (OpenVDDK.nbd.sessions, 1 to 16, default 1), so a single reader gets parallel transfers without a wrapper.

Quick to open and close

Opening a disk takes about a second and handing it back a fraction of a second in our measurements. Sequential readers get read-ahead, including programs that read asynchronously, such as nbdkit's VDDK plugin under virt-v2v.

Read-only by design

OpenVDDK reads disks for backup and migration and cannot write to them. Write calls return the same read-only error as VMware's library.

Talks only to your vSphere

It connects only to the vCenter and ESXi hosts your tool points it at. No telemetry; nothing is sent anywhere else.

Measurements

How to read these figures. They are our own measurements in our own labs, not an independent benchmark. Each comparison used the same application build, the same VM, worker and storage, and swapped only the library file; most are single runs or pairs.

Results depend on your storage, network, CPU and application. In your environment the two libraries may perform the same, and in the cases listed under Where VMware's library was faster, OpenVDDK was slower. Please measure in your own setup. Ask us for the method in a GitHub issue.

Single operations on physical ESXi 8.0.3 hosts, read over HotAdd, with only the library file swapped.

Read rate, 200 GiB disk

2,488 MiB/s

Opening a 40 GB disk

1.0 s

Handing the disk back

0.3 s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3: 12.6 s

Data read

Identical

Same SHA-256, both libraries

The 200 GiB disk was read with one request in flight and gave the same SHA-256 through both libraries, for the whole disk and for all 800 ranges. Opening and closing were measured on a 40 GB disk on VMFS from the same worker, two runs each; these times depend on vCenter and the ESXi host.

In a warm migration of a running 20 GB Debian 13 VM under V2K Migrate, a free, self-hosted VMware-to-KVM migration tool (a full baseline, two Changed Block Tracking deltas of 2 GiB and 5 GiB, and the final pass after shutdown), OpenVDDK completed the four passes in 118 s. Every pass carried the same bytes with both libraries, V2K Migrate's data check passed, and the changed files hash identically in both migrated VMs. VMware's library took 330 s for the same four passes. At the time, every name lookup on our lab's workers waited 5 s for a DNS server that did not answer. VMware's library made four such lookups in each disk open (39 s, against 19 s once the DNS server was fixed); OpenVDDK's disk open looks up no name. V2K Migrate's own vCenter connections waited the same way with both libraries.

ESXi and vCenter 8.0.3. Read rate: worker VM with 3 vCPUs and 4 GiB, NFS 4.1 datastore backed by RAM over 100 GbE, single runs, 3 October 2026; the gain applies to a reader with one request in flight. Open and close: worker VM with 8 vCPUs, VMFS datastore on an iSCSI LUN, 8 October 2026.

A real migration on a storage array

Cold migration of a 200 GiB Windows Server 2019 VM with V2K Migrate: the disk is read over HotAdd from a NetApp NFS datastore and written as a qcow2 file to an NFS export on the same NetApp. Same V2K Migrate build, same VM, same worker, same settings; only the library file was swapped.

Copy rate, 200 GiB

537 MiB/s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3: 282 MiB/s

Copy phase

381 s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3: 727 s

Waiting for reads

~182 s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3: 594 s

Output images

Identical

qemu-img compare, both qcow2 files

Both runs wrote exactly the same data: 181.3 GB to the qcow2 file and 33.4 GB of zeros skipped. V2K Migrate's data check passed both times, and qemu-img compare of the two output files reported them identical. The copier reads a block, writes it, then reads the next one: with VMware's library it spent 594 of the copy's 727 seconds waiting for reads, with OpenVDDK about 182 of 381 seconds. Most of the time now goes to writing the qcow2 file.

The whole migration took 7 min 24 s with OpenVDDK and 15 min 2 s with VMware's library. The same 5 s name-lookup wait applied: VMware's library made four lookups in its disk open and one in each of its seven allocated-block queries. Closing the disk, reading and the copy figures above were not affected.

Screenshot: the V2K Migrate worker's journal, filtered and shortened with the command shown at the top; internal names in the command are covered with grey bars. OpenVix: was the library's development log prefix up to 0.6.7; from 0.6.8 on it logs OpenVDDK: VixDiskLib: …. The MiB/s figure printed inside the log ("inside Read") counts only the time the application spent inside the library's read calls; with read-ahead the data is mostly in memory before it is asked for, so it is not a transfer rate. The real rate is the copy rate above.

ESXi and vCenter 8.0.3; worker VM with 3 vCPUs and 4 GiB on the source VM's host; NetApp NFS v3 datastore, destination over NFS 4.2 with 1 MiB transfers. Single run per library, 4 October 2026. The source datastore's NFS version made no difference: the same disk on an NFS 4.1 datastore of the same NetApp gave the same read rate.

How the hardware behaved

The worker VM and its ESXi host were sampled every two seconds during both runs. The full side-by-side profiler report is linked below; the main figures:

OpenVDDKVMware VDDK 8.0.3
Disk reads inside the worker, average / peak461 / 967 MiB/s227 / 616 MiB/s
Worker CPU busy, average37.8 %18.4 %
Worker memory used, average0.73 GiB0.70 GiB
ESXi host CPU, average12.9 %11.5 %
Read latency per request at ESXi, average18.8 ms2.5 ms
  • Twice the data per second, the same total work. The worker's CPU was twice as busy for half as long: CPU busy × duration comes to the same amount within 1 % for both runs. The ESXi host's CPU barely changed.
  • Memory did not change: the read-ahead keeps a few 2 MiB blocks in flight, not the disk.
  • The higher latency per request is how the speed is gained. VMware's library asks for one 1 MiB block at a time, so each request finds an empty queue (2.5 ms). OpenVDDK keeps several 2 MiB requests in flight; each waits longer in the queue (18.8 ms), and twice as much data arrives per second.
  • The worker's I/O wait rose with it (average 40 % against 18 %): it is writing the qcow2 file over NFS twice as fast and waits for those writes more often.
  • Both runs show a few dropped incoming network frames (58 and 120), at the same rate of about one every 7.6 seconds on both of the worker's network cards, including the idle management card: background frames the guest discards, not lost migration data.

Both graphs of a pair share the same time axis, in seconds from the start of each migration plan; the grey area is the time after the OpenVDDK run had already finished. VMware's run starts copying later, partly because of the name-lookup waits described above.

NBDSSL and NBD on vSphere 8.0.3

The same disks read over the network transports, with the tools that use them: nbdkit's VDDK plugin with virt-v2v's settings, and virt-v2v itself. Same worker, same disks; only the library file was swapped.

SHA-256 of every disk, both libraries

In these tests, both libraries read the same bytes over HotAdd, NBDSSL and NBD, with the same allocated-block maps, the same metadata and the same error codes. virt-v2v converted the guest with either library, every connection over NBDSSL. With one reader at a time OpenVDDK was 14 to 42 % faster; with four readers of one disk at once the two were on par, the difference going either way with the load on the storage.

In one four-reader NBDSSL-only test on vSphere 8.0.3 (9 October 2026), three of the four connections made with VMware VDDK 8.0.3 used clear-text NBD without reporting an error. OpenVDDK kept all four connections on NBDSSL.

ESXi and vCenter 8.0.3; worker VM with 8 vCPUs and 16 GiB; a NetApp NFS v3 datastore and a VMFS datastore on a RAM-backed iSCSI LUN; 20 GiB disks; nbdkit 1.38.5 with virt-v2v's filters and 64 requests in flight, virt-v2v 2.7.1. Copy-phase figures from two runs (9 and 15 October 2026), read rates from one series (9 October 2026), each library run twice in alternating order. Measured on a worker whose CPU exposes AES instructions, as servers and most virtual machines do.

One disk over several NFC sessions

Since 0.7.3, OpenVDDK can read one disk over several NFC sessions at once (OpenVDDK.nbd.sessions) and with larger transfer buffers, using VMware's documented key vixDiskLib.nfcAio.Session.BufSizeIn64KB. Same physical vSphere 8.0.3 worker and disk for every run; only the library and its settings changed.

NBDSSL, one disk, 4 sessions and 2 MiB buffers

927 MiB/s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3 at its best setting (default): 275 MiB/s

NBDSSL, one disk, default settings

300 MiB/s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3: 275 MiB/s

Whole 20 GiB disk through nbdkit, one request at a time, as CloudStack's import uses it

203 MiB/s

VMware VDDK 8.0.3: 88 MiB/s

Data

Identical

SHA-256 of the whole disk, both libraries

With its own 2 MiB buffer key, VMware's library read this disk at 224 MiB/s, slower than its default, and its log does not show the buffer size it used. The comparison therefore uses its best result, the default. VMware's library reads a disk over one session; it has no setting to spread one disk over several.

Every session uses part of the ESXi host's NFC memory, with either library. With 2 MiB buffers, each session takes about 4 MiB of it. A default host has 96 MiB. In our lab tests, a default host served 16 such sessions and refused a 24th, with either library; with default buffers, 40 readers at once ran fine. So with 4 sessions and 2 MiB buffers, plan on up to about 4 disks at once per ESXi host. The host's NFC memory can be raised (VMware KB 389223); in a lab test, doubling it doubled the number of sessions the host served. Changing a host setting is the host owner's decision.

ESXi and vCenter 8.0.3, physical hosts; worker VM with 3 vCPUs and 3.6 GiB, whose CPU exposes AES instructions; an NFS datastore; a 20 GiB disk. Read rates: 8 GiB per run, median of three runs in rotated order (3 November 2026). The nbdkit stream: the whole disk once per library, with nbdkit's VDDK plugin as virt-v2v starts it.

Where VMware's library was faster

  • NBDSSL on a CPU without AES instructions. Some virtual machines are given a CPU model that hides them. NBDSSL then decrypts in software, which slows both libraries and OpenVDDK more: in a test on a physical ESXi 8.0.3 host, OpenVDDK read at 102–104 MiB/s against 158–176 MiB/s with VMware's library. OpenVDDK logs a warning at open naming the fix: give the reader VM the host's CPU features. NBD is not affected.
  • Several readers of one disk at once. With four readers the two libraries were on par; the difference went either way with the load on the storage.
  • A path that limits both libraries. Reading with nothing to do between reads, over iSCSI VMFS at MTU 1500 (about 1.0 GB/s), VMware's library was about 3 % faster.

What comes next

  • Encrypted VMs over plain NBD: switching to an encrypted connection automatically, as VMware's library does (0.7.5).
  • A home in a neutral open-source foundation: in discussion.
  • HotAdd on a standalone ESXi host: considered for 0.7.5.
  • OpenNebula has accepted adding OpenVDDK support to its OneSwap migration tool, planned for OpenNebula 7.6 (OpenNebula/one#8159).

OpenVDDK is free and will stay free. Download the kits from the GitHub release: a user kit for running existing tools, a developer kit for writing your own. Or build it from source.

Get notified about new releases

Leave your email and we'll tell you when a new OpenVDDK version is out: what changed and where to download it. Downloads need no sign-up. Telling us which software or project you use it with helps us decide what to test next. Download links you received earlier keep working.

Also on GitHub. Found a bug or tested it with your tool? Open a GitHub issue. Security reports: see SECURITY.md for private reporting via [email protected] or GitHub's private reporting where enabled.

content_html_zh:
Open source · Apache 2.0 · HotAdd, NBDSSL and NBD

Independent Virtual Disk LibraryDrop-in. Written from scratch.

OpenVDDK is an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.

Note: the README inside the 0.7.4 download lists vSphere 6.7, 7.0 and 8.0. vSphere 9.1.1 was tested after the release (see "Where it stands"). We don't change released files, so their published SHA-256 checksums, and installers that rely on them, stay valid. The next release carries the updated list.

Your application doesn't have to know

An application that loads libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3 doesn't need to know whether it got VMware's VDDK or OpenVDDK: same file name, same functions, same calls, same data back. No rewrite and no new integration path. In our tests, the difference applications noticed was the timing.

Same file, same interface

The same shared object name and the same exported VixDiskLib functions. Replace the file and restart the service.

HotAdd

Attaches the snapshot disk to your proxy VM, finds and verifies it in the guest, reads it and hands it back. An interrupted run is cleaned up by the next one.

NBDSSL and NBD

Reads the disk directly from the ESXi host over NBDSSL or NBD, without a HotAdd proxy VM. NBDSSL encrypts the connection. Only the transports you request are used: an NBDSSL-only request never falls back to clear-text NBD. A disk can be read over several NFC sessions at once (OpenVDDK.nbd.sessions, 1 to 16, default 1), so a single reader gets parallel transfers without a wrapper.

Quick to open and close

Opening a disk takes about a second and handing it back a fraction of a second in our measurements. Sequential readers get read-ahead, including programs that read asynchronously, such as nbdkit's VDDK plugin under virt-v2v.

设计为只读

OpenVDDK reads disks for backup and migration and cannot write to them. Write calls return the same read-only error as VMware's library.

Talks only to your vSphere

It connects only to the vCenter and ESXi hosts your tool points it at. No telemetry; nothing is sent anywhere else.

Measurements

How to read these figures. They are our own measurements in our own labs, not an independent benchmark. Each comparison used the same application build, the same VM, worker and storage, and swapped only the library file; most are single runs or pairs.

Results depend on your storage, network, CPU and application. In your environment the two libraries may perform the same, and in the cases listed under Where VMware's library was faster, OpenVDDK was slower. Please measure in your own setup. Ask us for the method in a GitHub issue.

Same SHA-256, both libraries

The 200 GiB disk was read with one request in flight and gave the same SHA-256 through both libraries, for the whole disk and for all 800 ranges. Opening and closing were measured on a 40 GB disk on VMFS from the same worker, two runs each; these times depend on vCenter and the ESXi host.

In a warm migration of a running 20 GB Debian 13 VM under V2K Migrate, a free, self-hosted VMware-to-KVM migration tool (a full baseline, two Changed Block Tracking deltas of 2 GiB and 5 GiB, and the final pass after shutdown), OpenVDDK completed the four passes in 118 s. Every pass carried the same bytes with both libraries, V2K Migrate's data check passed, and the changed files hash identically in both migrated VMs. VMware's library took 330 s for the same four passes. At the time, every name lookup on our lab's workers waited 5 s for a DNS server that did not answer. VMware's library made four such lookups in each disk open (39 s, against 19 s once the DNS server was fixed); OpenVDDK's disk open looks up no name. V2K Migrate's own vCenter connections waited the same way with both libraries.

Both runs wrote exactly the same data: 181.3 GB to the qcow2 file and 33.4 GB of zeros skipped. V2K Migrate's data check passed both times, and qemu-img compare of the two output files reported them identical. The copier reads a block, writes it, then reads the next one: with VMware's library it spent 594 of the copy's 727 seconds waiting for reads, with OpenVDDK about 182 of 381 seconds. Most of the time now goes to writing the qcow2 file.

The whole migration took 7 min 24 s with OpenVDDK and 15 min 2 s with VMware's library. The same 5 s name-lookup wait applied: VMware's library made four lookups in its disk open and one in each of its seven allocated-block queries. Closing the disk, reading and the copy figures above were not affected.

Screenshot: the V2K Migrate worker's journal, filtered and shortened with the command shown at the top; internal names in the command are covered with grey bars. OpenVix: was the library's development log prefix up to 0.6.7; from 0.6.8 on it logs OpenVDDK: VixDiskLib: …. The MiB/s figure printed inside the log ("inside Read") counts only the time the application spent inside the library's read calls; with read-ahead the data is mostly in memory before it is asked for, so it is not a transfer rate. The real rate is the copy rate above.

The source datastore's NFS version made no difference: the same disk on an NFS 4.1 datastore of the same NetApp gave the same read rate.

How the hardware behaved

The worker VM and its ESXi host were sampled every two seconds during both runs. The full side-by-side profiler report is linked below; the main figures:

  • Twice the data per second, the same total work. The worker's CPU was twice as busy for half as long: CPU busy × duration comes to the same amount within 1 % for both runs. The ESXi host's CPU barely changed.
  • Memory did not change: the read-ahead keeps a few 2 MiB blocks in flight, not the disk.
  • The higher latency per request is how the speed is gained. VMware's library asks for one 1 MiB block at a time, so each request finds an empty queue (2.5 ms). OpenVDDK keeps several 2 MiB requests in flight; each waits longer in the queue (18.8 ms), and twice as much data arrives per second.
  • The worker's I/O wait rose with it (average 40 % against 18 %): it is writing the qcow2 file over NFS twice as fast and waits for those writes more often.
  • Both runs show a few dropped incoming network frames (58 and 120), at the same rate of about one every 7.6 seconds on both of the worker's network cards, including the idle management card: background frames the guest discards, not lost migration data.

With its own 2 MiB buffer key, VMware's library read this disk at 224 MiB/s, slower than its default, and its log does not show the buffer size it used. The comparison therefore uses its best result, the default. VMware's library reads a disk over one session; it has no setting to spread one disk over several.

Every session uses part of the ESXi host's NFC memory, with either library. With 2 MiB buffers, each session takes about 4 MiB of it. A default host has 96 MiB. In our lab tests, a default host served 16 such sessions and refused a 24th, with either library; with default buffers, 40 readers at once ran fine. So with 4 sessions and 2 MiB buffers, plan on up to about 4 disks at once per ESXi host. The host's NFC memory can be raised (VMware KB 389223); in a lab test, doubling it doubled the number of sessions the host served. Changing a host setting is the host owner's decision.

Where VMware's library was faster

  • NBDSSL on a CPU without AES instructions. Some virtual machines are given a CPU model that hides them. NBDSSL then decrypts in software, which slows both libraries and OpenVDDK more: in a test on a physical ESXi 8.0.3 host, OpenVDDK read at 102–104 MiB/s against 158–176 MiB/s with VMware's library. OpenVDDK logs a warning at open naming the fix: give the reader VM the host's CPU features. NBD is not affected.
  • Several readers of one disk at once. With four readers the two libraries were on par; the difference went either way with the load on the storage.
  • A path that limits both libraries. Reading with nothing to do between reads, over iSCSI VMFS at MTU 1500 (about 1.0 GB/s), VMware's library was about 3 % faster.
